pos: n. (father of Abram, Nahor and Haran; an idolater out of Ur who began the journey to Canaan and stopped short of it)
etymology: From Hebrew Terach, of uncertain derivation. Luke's genealogy renders the name Thara. The man is remembered less for what the name means than for where he stopped.
biblical_def: Terah is the father of Abram, and Joshua tells Israel plainly what he was: “Your fathers dwelt on the other side of the flood in old time, even Terah, the father of Abraham, and the father of Nachor: and they served other gods” (Jos 24:2). The line of promise begins in a house of idols. That is the first thing to say about Terah, and it is the reason Abram's call is called grace and not merit. The second thing is stranger. Terah himself set out: “Terah took Abram his son, and Lot the son of Haran his son's son, and Sarai his daughter in law… and they went forth with them from Ur of the Chaldees, to go into the land of Canaan” (Gen 11:31). The destination is named. He intended Canaan. And the verse ends: “they came unto Haran, and dwelt there”. He got halfway, found a place that suited him, and settled. “The days of Terah were two hundred and five years: and Terah died in Haran” (Gen 11:32). Only after his death does God's word come again and Abram go on. Terah is the man who left Ur and never reached Canaan — not because the road closed, but because Haran was comfortable. Scripture never says he sinned in stopping. It simply records that he stopped, and lets the record speak.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Terah; in sacred history he is the father of Abram, Nahor and Haran, an idolater of Ur who removed to Haran and died there.
webster_full: TERAH, n. The son of Nahor, and the father of Abram, Nahor and Haran.
He dwelt in Ur of the Chaldees, and served other gods, as Joshua testifies.
He took his family and departed from Ur, intending to go into the land of Canaan.
Coming to Haran, he dwelt there, and did not proceed further.
He died in Haran, being two hundred and five years old.
scriptures: And Terah lived seventy years, and begat Abram, Nahor, and Haran.

And Terah took Abram his son, and Lot the son of Haran his son's son, and Sarai his daughter in law, his son Abram's wife; and they went forth with them from Ur of the Chaldees, to go into the land of Canaan; and they came unto Haran, and dwelt there.
And the days of Terah were two hundred and five years: and Terah died in Haran.
Jos 24:2

And Joshua said unto all the people, Thus saith the LORD God of Israel, Your fathers dwelt on the other side of the flood in old time, even Terah, the father of Abraham, and the father of Nachor: and they served other gods.
corruption_summary: Abraham's ancestry is sanitized into a monotheistic heritage he inherited, when Scripture says his father served other gods — and the sanitizing quietly turns free election into family tradition.
corruption_paragraphs: A widespread popular telling makes Abraham the heir of a purer faith, or the lone monotheist in an idolatrous age who reasoned his way to the true God. Joshua flatly contradicts the first: Terah served other gods. And Scripture nowhere credits Abram with discovering anything. The initiative is entirely on the other side — “The God of glory appeared unto our father Abraham, when he was in Mesopotamia, before he dwelt in Charran” (Act 7:2). Sovereign grace reached into an idolater's household and took a man out of it. That is the doctrine the passage exists to teach, and every retelling that gives Abram a head start destroys it. Israel is told this at the covenant renewal precisely so that the nation will never think itself chosen for its pedigree.

The second corruption is a sentimentality that turns Terah into a hero for starting. He did start, and the text gives him that credit without comment. But it also records where he stopped, and Haran is not Canaan. There is a manner of religion that leaves the old country without ever arriving at the promise — out of Ur, short of the land, settled in a place with the family name on it and the old gods within reach. Scripture's word for the alternative is endurance: “we are made partakers of Christ, if we hold the beginning of our confidence stedfast unto the end” (Heb 3:14). Terah is not condemned in the record. He is simply left in Haran, and the story goes on without him.
roots_summary: Hebrew Terach (H8646), Terah; 'Ur (H218), Ur; Charan (H2771), Haran; yashab (H3427), to dwell, settle; 'elohim 'acherim, other gods.

Hebrew 'Ur (H218) — Ur of the Chaldees, the city he left.
Hebrew Charan (H2771) — Haran, the city he stopped in and died in.
Hebrew yashab (H3427) — to sit, remain, dwell, settle; the verb of Gen 11:31's last clause.
Hebrew 'acher (H312) — other, another; in the phrase “other gods” of Jos 24:2.
usage: “They served other gods” — the household grace reached into.
“To go into the land of Canaan; and they came unto Haran, and dwelt there” — the whole tragedy in one verse.
“Terah died in Haran” — halfway, and comfortable.

pos: n. (son of Nahor and Milcah, father of Rebekah and Laban; the Aramean kinsman through whom the patriarchal wives came)
etymology: From Hebrew Bethu'el, commonly explained as “man of God” or “dweller in God”. He lived in Padanaram, and the household kept the family gods alongside the family name.
biblical_def: Bethuel is the bridge between Abraham's house and the wives of the next two generations. Son of Nahor by Milcah, he is introduced with a note of purpose: “And Bethuel begat Rebekah: these eight Milcah did bear to Nahor, Abraham's brother” (Gen 22:23) — recorded immediately after the binding of Isaac, as though the reader should already be asking where Isaac's wife will come from. When Abraham's servant is sent to find her, the answer arrives before he has finished praying: “behold, Rebekah came out, who was born to Bethuel, son of Milcah, the wife of Nahor, Abraham's brother” (Gen 24:15). Bethuel's single recorded speech is a confession of providence. Faced with a servant's account of a prayer answered at a well, he and Laban say together: “The thing proceedeth from the LORD: we cannot speak unto thee bad or good” (Gen 24:50). A generation later Isaac sends Jacob back to the same house — “Arise, go to Padanaram, to the house of Bethuel thy mother's father” (Gen 28:2) — and from it come Leah and Rachel and the twelve tribes. One Aramean household, three generations of covenant marriages, and a father who recognized the hand of God when he saw it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Bethuel; in sacred history he is the son of Nahor and Milcah, and the father of Rebekah and Laban.
webster_full: BETHUEL, n. The son of Nahor, the brother of Abraham, by Milcah his wife.
He was the father of Rebekah, who became the wife of Isaac, and of Laban the Syrian.
He dwelt in Padanaram, in Mesopotamia, whither Abraham sent his servant to seek a wife for his son.
With Laban he acknowledged that the matter proceeded from the LORD.
Jacob was afterward sent to his house to take a wife of the daughters of Laban.
scriptures: And Bethuel begat Rebekah: these eight Milcah did bear to Nahor, Abraham's brother.
And it came to pass, before he had done speaking, that, behold, Rebekah came out, who was born to Bethuel, son of Milcah, the wife of Nahor, Abraham's brother, with her pitcher upon her shoulder.
Then Laban and Bethuel answered and said, The thing proceedeth from the LORD: we cannot speak unto thee bad or good.
Gen 28:2
Arise, go to Padanaram, to the house of Bethuel thy mother's father; and take thee a wife from thence of the daughters of Laban thy mother's brother.
corruption_summary: Abraham's insistence that Isaac not marry a Canaanite is read as ethnic prejudice, when the concern named in the text is worship — and the modern church has largely stopped applying the principle at all.
corruption_paragraphs: Abraham makes his servant swear not to take a wife for Isaac of the daughters of the Canaanites, and modern readers commonly file this as tribal endogamy. The text gives a different reason and gives it repeatedly: the Canaanite houses were houses of Molech and Ashtoreth, and the covenant seed was not to be joined to them. The concern is worship, not blood — which is why Rahab the Canaanite and Ruth the Moabitess are welcomed into Israel and into the line of Christ, both by way of confession. The New Testament keeps the principle and drops the geography: “Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers” (2Co 6:14), and a widow is free to marry whom she will, “only in the Lord” (1Co 7:39).

The second corruption is neglect rather than distortion. Bethuel's house was chosen because it still knew the name of the LORD, however imperfectly — and imperfectly it was, for Rachel would later steal her father's images out of it. Even so, a father in that generation crossed four hundred miles to secure a believing marriage for his son. Much of the modern church has quietly abandoned the concern, treating a spouse's faith as a preference rather than a boundary, and then wondering at the state of its children. The dictionary holds that marriage is a covenant before God between one man and one woman, and that whom a believer marries is a matter of obedience, not taste.

Hebrew tob (H2896) — good; in the idiom “we cannot speak unto thee bad or good”, a refusal to contradict God.
usage: “The thing proceedeth from the LORD” — a father recognizing providence and yielding to it.
“Before he had done speaking… Rebekah came out” — the answer overtaking the prayer.
“The house of Bethuel thy mother's father” — one household, three generations of covenant marriages.

pos: n. (the Hittite of Hebron who sold Abraham the cave of Machpelah, the first piece of the promised land ever owned by the covenant family)
etymology: From Hebrew 'Ephron, connected with 'epher, dust or ashes — fitting for the man who sold a grave. He is always identified by his people: Ephron the Hittite, son of Zohar.
biblical_def: Ephron owned a field at Machpelah before Mamre, and Abraham came to him as a stranger and a sojourner needing to bury Sarah. The negotiation in Genesis 23 is one of the most carefully reported transactions in the Bible, and every detail of it matters. Ephron offers the field as a gift in the hearing of all who went in at the gate of his city (Gen 23:10) — the courteous eastern opening that expects a price to follow — and names the figure almost in passing: four hundred shekels of silver, what is that between me and thee. Abraham does not haggle and does not accept a gift: “Abraham weighed to Ephron the silver, which he had named in the audience of the sons of Heth, four hundred shekels of silver, current money with the merchant” (Gen 23:16). Weighed, publicly, at the named price, before witnesses at the gate. The patriarch who had been promised the whole land bought one field in it, at full value, for a grave — and that cave became the burying place of Sarah, Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah, Leah and Jacob (Gen 49:30-31). The first title deed the covenant family held in Canaan was a tomb, purchased from a Hittite, and it was enough to hold their bones until God gave the rest.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Ephron; in sacred history he is the Hittite, son of Zohar, who sold to Abraham the field and cave of Machpelah for a burying place.
webster_full: EPHRON, n. The son of Zohar, a Hittite dwelling at Hebron among the children of Heth.
He was the owner of the field of Machpelah, and of the cave that was therein.
He offered the field to Abraham as a gift, in the audience of the people at the gate.
Abraham weighed to him four hundred shekels of silver, current money with the merchant.
The field and cave were thus made sure unto Abraham for a possession of a buryingplace.
scriptures: And Ephron dwelt among the children of Heth: and Ephron the Hittite answered Abraham in the audience of the children of Heth, even of all that went in at the gate of his city, saying,
And Abraham hearkened unto Ephron; and Abraham weighed to Ephron the silver, which he had named in the audience of the sons of Heth, four hundred shekels of silver, current money with the merchant.
Gen 25:9
And his sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him in the cave of Machpelah, in the field of Ephron the son of Zohar the Hittite, which is before Mamre;
In the cave that is in the field of Machpelah, which is before Mamre, in the land of Canaan, which Abraham bought with the field of Ephron the Hittite for a possession of a buryingplace.
corruption_summary: The purchase is read either as a mere property record with no theology in it, or as evidence that the promise of the land was symbolic all along; Genesis presents it as faith holding a deed against a promise not yet kept.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 23 is sometimes treated as an archival curiosity — an ancient conveyance preserved by accident. But the chapter is deliberate, and its deliberateness is the doctrine. Abraham had been promised the land by God and owned none of it. He refused a gift because a gift can be revoked and because he would not have it said that a Hittite had enriched him; he insisted on a weighed, witnessed, full-price purchase; and what he bought was a grave. Hebrews explains the frame of mind: he “sojourned in the land of promise, as in a strange country”, looking for a city whose builder and maker is God (Heb 11:9-10). The deed is faith's down payment on a word not yet fulfilled.

The opposite error takes the smallness of the purchase as evidence that the land promise was never really territorial — a spiritual figure from the start. Scripture will not have that either. God said to Abram, “Unto thy seed have I given this land” (Gen 15:18), and the conquest under Joshua is recorded as its fulfilment: “There failed not ought of any good thing which the LORD had spoken unto the house of Israel; all came to pass” (Jos 21:45). The dictionary holds both together without embarrassment — a real land given to a real nation, and a better country, that is, an heavenly, which the patriarchs were seeking all along and which the purchase of one grave quietly confessed.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'Ephron (H6085), Ephron; Makpelah (H4375), Machpelah; shaqal (H8254), to weigh; 'achuzzah (H272), possession; ger (H1616), stranger, sojourner.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'Ephron (H6085) — Ephron; the Hittite owner of the field at Machpelah.
Hebrew Makpelah (H4375) — Machpelah, the double cave; the burying place of the patriarchs.
Hebrew shaqal (H8254) — to weigh out; Abraham weighed the silver rather than take a gift.
Hebrew 'achuzzah (H272) — possession, holding; the legal term for what the purchase secured.
Hebrew ger (H1616) — stranger, sojourner; Abraham's own description of himself among them.
usage: “Abraham weighed to Ephron the silver” — full price, in public, before witnesses.
“Current money with the merchant” — no discount, no favour, no debt.
The first acre of the promised land the covenant family owned was a grave.

pos: n. (third son of Judah by the daughter of Shua; the son withheld from Tamar, and head of the Shelanite family in Judah)
etymology: From Hebrew Shelah, connected with a root meaning to draw out or to be at rest. He is not to be confused with Salah son of Arphaxad, whose name the KJV spells differently.
biblical_def: Shelah is Judah's third son, born at Chezib (Gen 38:5), and his part in the narrative is entirely passive — he is the son who was promised and never given. Er and Onan, his elder brothers, were both slain by the LORD for wickedness, and by the custom later written into the law the widow Tamar had a right to the next brother. Judah made the promise and then hedged it: “Remain a widow at thy father's house, till Shelah my son be grown: for he said, Lest peradventure he die also, as his brethren did” (Gen 38:11). The parenthesis exposes him. Judah is not protecting Tamar; he is protecting Shelah from Tamar, whom he privately blames for two deaths that Scripture blames on his sons. Years pass. “She saw that Shelah was grown, and she was not given unto him to wife” (Gen 38:14) — and out of that broken promise comes Tamar's desperate stratagem, Judah's exposure, and the birth of Pharez, through whom David and the Lord Jesus descend. Shelah survives it all. He goes down into Egypt with the seventy (Gen 46:12), and the Shelanites are counted in the wilderness census as a family of Judah. The son who was withheld to protect the line was not the son the line ran through.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Shelah; in sacred history he is the third son of Judah, whom his father withheld from Tamar, and the head of the family of the Shelanites.
webster_full: SHELAH, n. The third son of Judah by the daughter of Shua the Canaanite, born at Chezib.
He is to be distinguished from Salah, the son of Arphaxad, in the line of Shem.
Judah promised him to Tamar, the widow of his brethren Er and Onan, but did not give him.
He went down with Jacob into Egypt among the sons of Judah.
From him descended the family of the Shelanites, numbered among the tribe of Judah.
scriptures: Gen 38:5
And she yet again conceived, and bare a son; and called his name Shelah: and he was at Chezib, when she bare him.

Then said Judah to Tamar his daughter in law, Remain a widow at thy father's house, till Shelah my son be grown: for he said, Lest peradventure he die also, as his brethren did. And Tamar went and dwelt in her father's house.

And she put her widow's garments off from her, and covered her with a vail, and wrapped herself, and sat in an open place, which is by the way to Timnath; for she saw that Shelah was grown, and she was not given unto him to wife.
And the sons of Judah; Er, and Onan, and Shelah, and Pharez, and Zerah: but Er and Onan died in the land of Canaan. And the sons of Pharez were Hezron and Hamul.
corruption_summary: Judah's withholding of Shelah is treated as prudent fatherhood rather than as the breach of duty Judah himself later confesses, and the levirate obligation is dismissed as primitive custom.
corruption_paragraphs: Read superficially, Judah looks careful: two sons dead, a third to protect. Scripture reads him otherwise, and so eventually does he. The deaths were judicial — Er “was wicked in the sight of the LORD; and the LORD slew him” (Gen 38:7) — and had nothing to do with Tamar. Judah left a widow in her father's house under a promise he had no intention of keeping, which in that world meant a life without protection, provision or children. When the truth came out he did not defend himself: “She hath been more righteous than I; because that I gave her not to Shelah my son” (Gen 38:26). The narrative asks the reader to see what Judah eventually saw — that a broken promise to a defenceless woman is not caution but injustice, and that God had noticed.

The levirate duty itself is commonly waved off as an artefact of a primitive society. But the law that Moses later codified (Deu 25:5-6) exists to protect exactly the person least able to protect herself, and to keep a dead man's name in Israel. It is the same instinct that produces the kinsman-redeemer, and it runs straight to Boaz, who performed for Ruth what Judah refused to Tamar — and to Christ, who is not ashamed to call us brethren and who redeems what we could not. A society is measured by what it does for the widow: “Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction” (Jas 1:27).

“She saw that Shelah was grown, and she was not given unto him to wife” — the years counted by the wronged.
The son withheld to save the line was not the son the line came through.

pos: n. (elder twin of Judah and Tamar, ancestor of Boaz, David and the Lord Jesus Christ; the KJV New Testament spells the name Phares)
etymology: From Hebrew Perets, a breach or bursting forth, from parats, to break through — named from the manner of his birth, when he broke out ahead of the brother whose hand had appeared first.
biblical_def: Pharez was born out of the ugliest episode in the patriarchal narratives and stands at the head of the royal line. Tamar, twice widowed and cheated of Shelah, disguised herself and conceived by Judah her father-in-law; and at the birth the midwife bound a scarlet thread on the hand that came first, and then the other child broke past him: “behold, his brother came out: and she said, How hast thou broken forth? this breach be upon thee: therefore his name was called Pharez” (Gen 38:29). The younger displaces the elder yet again — as with Isaac, Jacob, Ephraim and David — and the line runs through the one no one expected. Ruth ends with his genealogy: “Now these are the generations of Pharez: Pharez begat Hezron” (Rut 4:18), and ten names later, David. Matthew opens the New Testament with the same names and does not hide the mother: “Judas begat Phares and Zara of Thamar” (Mat 1:3). Four women are named in that genealogy and every one of them carries a scandal or a foreign birth. The evangelist could have left them out. He put them in, because the point of the line is not the dignity of the ancestors but the mercy of the God who used them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Pharez; in sacred history he is the son of Judah by Tamar, twin brother of Zerah, and an ancestor of David and of Christ.
webster_full: PHAREZ, n. The elder of the twin sons of Judah by Tamar his daughter in law.
The name signifies a breach, and was given him because he broke forth before his brother Zerah.
His sons were Hezron and Hamul, who went down into Egypt with Jacob.
From Hezron descend Ram, Amminadab, Nahshon, Salmon, Boaz, Obed, Jesse and David.
In the New Testament the name is written Phares, in the genealogy of our Lord.
scriptures: And it came to pass, as he drew back his hand, that, behold, his brother came out: and she said, How hast thou broken forth? this breach be upon thee: therefore his name was called Pharez.
And Tamar his daughter in law bare him Pharez and Zerah. All the sons of Judah were five.
Rut 4:18
Now these are the generations of Pharez: Pharez begat Hezron,
Mat 1:3
And Judas begat Phares and Zara of Thamar; and Phares begat Esrom; and Esrom begat Aram;
corruption_summary: The genealogy of Christ is either sanitized by silence about its scandals or turned into a warrant for excusing sin, when Scripture names the sins plainly and magnifies the grace that worked through them.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite handlings of this line are common, and both miss it. The first is embarrassed silence — the Christmas genealogy read quickly, Tamar and Rahab and Bathsheba passed over, the impression left that the Lord's ancestry was respectable. The second, more modern, uses the same names to argue that God is indifferent to the sin, as though the presence of scandal in the line made the scandal acceptable. Scripture does neither. It records Judah's sin as sin and his confession as confession; it never softens Genesis 38; and it puts Tamar in Matthew 1 with her name attached. The doctrine is that grace reaches into real filth and brings a Redeemer out of it, which is a very different thing from grace approving of filth. “Where sin abounded, grace did much more abound” (Rom 5:20) — followed immediately by Paul's own guard against the abuse: “Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid” (Rom 6:1-2).

There is a second correction to make, against a reading that treats the younger-displaces-elder pattern as a folk motif. It happens too often and too pointedly to be decoration. Isaac over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau, Ephraim over Manasseh, David over seven brothers, Pharez over Zerah — the God of Scripture systematically refuses the claims of natural precedence, and Paul says why: “God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise… that no flesh should glory in his presence” (1Co 1:27-29). A breach-born son of an incestuous union heads the royal house, so that when the King finally comes no man can mistake His title for an inheritance of merit.

Hebrew parats (H6555) — to break out, break through, make a breach; the verb the midwife used.
Hebrew Zerach (H2226) — Zerah; his twin, whose hand appeared first and who was born second.
Hebrew toledoth (H8435) — generations; the heading of the closing genealogy of Ruth.
Greek Phares (G5329) — Phares; the form of the name in Matthew's and Luke's genealogies.

“Now these are the generations of Pharez” — the book of Ruth ends by pointing at David.
“Judas begat Phares and Zara of Thamar” — the evangelist names the mother and hides nothing.

pos: n. (second son of Judah, slain by the LORD for refusing his brother's widow the seed the duty required)
etymology: From Hebrew 'Onan, connected with 'on, strength or vigour, and by a homonym with sorrow. His name has been attached in later English to a sin the text does not principally charge him with.
biblical_def: Onan is the second son of Judah (Gen 38:4), and his whole history occupies three verses. When his elder brother Er was slain for wickedness, the duty of raising up seed to him fell on Onan, and Judah stated it plainly: “Go in unto thy brother's wife, and marry her, and raise up seed to thy brother” (Gen 38:8). Onan took the wife and refused the duty. The text is exact about his motive: “Onan knew that the seed should not be his; and it came to pass, when he went in unto his brother's wife, that he spilled it on the ground, lest that he should give seed to his brother” (Gen 38:9). He wanted the marriage without the obligation, the woman without the heir, and the inheritance undivided in his own line. It was calculated, repeated, and covetous. The verdict is one sentence: “And the thing which he did displeased the LORD: wherefore he slew him also” (Gen 38:10). Two brothers dead by the hand of God in the space of six verses, in the household of the man through whom the Messiah would come — and the shocking thing is that the line survives at all. It survives through Tamar, whom both of them wronged.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Onan; in sacred history he is the second son of Judah, slain by the LORD for refusing to raise up seed to his brother.
webster_full: ONAN, n. The second son of Judah by the daughter of Shua.
Upon the death of his elder brother Er, he was commanded to take Tamar and raise up seed to him.
He took her, but frustrated the purpose of the marriage, knowing the seed should not be his own.
The thing which he did displeased the LORD, and he was slain.
He died in the land of Canaan, before the going down into Egypt.
scriptures: Gen 38:4
And she conceived again, and bare a son; and she called his name Onan.
Gen 38:8
And Judah said unto Onan, Go in unto thy brother's wife, and marry her, and raise up seed to thy brother.
Gen 38:9
And Onan knew that the seed should not be his; and it came to pass, when he went in unto his brother's wife, that he spilled it on the ground, lest that he should give seed to his brother.
And the thing which he did displeased the LORD: wherefore he slew him also.
corruption_summary: The passage is regularly reduced to a proof-text about one bodily act while the sin Scripture actually names — covetous refusal of a duty owed to the dead and to the defenceless — is passed over.
corruption_paragraphs: The English word coined from this man's name has narrowed the passage until most readers assume the mechanics were the offence. Moses is more precise. He gives the motive twice in one verse — Onan knew the seed should not be his, and acted lest he should give seed to his brother. The sin is a settled, repeated, self-interested refusal of a duty God had laid on him: to preserve a dead brother's name and to give a defenceless widow a place in Israel. He took the privileges of the marriage and withheld its purpose, which is fraud as well as covetousness. The dictionary does not thereby license what the passage has traditionally been used against; Scripture has much to say elsewhere about purity of body and mind, and “every one that looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart” (Mat 5:28). It says only that a text should be made to say what it says.

The second corruption is the modern flinching at the verdict. God killed him, and readers want the sentence explained away as illness or coincidence. Genesis will not permit it: “the thing which he did displeased the LORD: wherefore he slew him also”. The God of Scripture is the living God who judges sin in real time when He pleases, as Ananias and Sapphira discovered in the age of grace itself (Act 5:5, 10). Modern religion has grown comfortable with a God who disapproves and does nothing. The Bible's God is holy, and the fear of Him is the beginning of wisdom: “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb 10:31).

Hebrew chamad (H2530) — to covet, desire; the root sin beneath the refusal, the inheritance kept whole.
usage: “Raise up seed to thy brother” — the duty stated in seven words.
“Lest that he should give seed to his brother” — Moses gives the motive, not merely the act.
“Wherefore he slew him also” — two brothers, six verses, one verdict.

pos: n. (the name of two women: the first wife of Lamech the Cainite, and a Hittite wife of Esau; both stand in households where marriage was corrupted)
etymology: From Hebrew 'Adah, ornament or adornment, from a root meaning to pass on or to deck oneself. The name is beautiful; the two households that bore it are not.
biblical_def: Adah is borne by two women, and Scripture places each of them at a point where the creation ordinance of marriage is being broken. The first is the elder of the two wives of Lamech, in the line of Cain: “Lamech took unto him two wives: the name of the one was Adah, and the name of the other Zillah” (Gen 4:19) — the first polygamy recorded in the Bible, appearing in the same short passage as the first boast of vengeance. Adah bore Jabal, “the father of such as dwell in tents, and of such as have cattle” (Gen 4:20), so the Cainite line produces real culture and real invention while producing real violence. The second Adah is a Hittite, one of the wives Esau took out of Canaan: “Adah the daughter of Elon the Hittite” (Gen 36:2), and she bore Eliphaz (Gen 36:4), whose son was Amalek. Isaac and Rebekah had been grieved to the soul by these marriages. Both Adahs therefore sit at the head of a line that will trouble the people of God — and Scripture, which could have omitted them, names them, records their sons, and lets the reader trace what came of households built against the pattern of Genesis 2.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Adah; in sacred history the name belongs to the first wife of Lamech in the line of Cain, and to a Hittite wife of Esau.
webster_full: ADAH, n. The name signifies ornament or beauty.
The first of the name was one of the two wives of Lamech, the descendant of Cain.
She bore Jabal, the father of such as dwell in tents and have cattle.
The second was the daughter of Elon the Hittite, and a wife of Esau.
She bore Eliphaz, from whom descended the dukes of Edom, and Amalek.

And Lamech took unto him two wives: the name of the one was Adah, and the name of the other Zillah.
Gen 4:20
And Adah bare Jabal: he was the father of such as dwell in tents, and of such as have cattle.
Gen 36:2
Esau took his wives of the daughters of Canaan; Adah the daughter of Elon the Hittite, and Aholibamah the daughter of Anah the daughter of Zibeon the Hivite;
Gen 36:4
And Adah bare to Esau Eliphaz; and Bashemath bare Reuel;
corruption_summary: The Bible's record of polygamy is offered as evidence that Scripture endorses plural marriage, or that marriage is a shifting cultural arrangement rather than a creation ordinance.
corruption_paragraphs: That the Bible records polygamy is beyond dispute; that it commends it is nowhere the case. The distinction between narration and approval has to be insisted on, because a great deal of argument depends on blurring it. The first polygamist in Scripture is Lamech, a murderer boasting of his vengeance to the two wives he had taken (Gen 4:23) — the account is a description of the corruption of Cain's line, not a model. And every later polygamous household in the canon is shown breeding exactly the misery you would expect: Sarah and Hagar, Leah and Rachel, Hannah and Peninnah, Solomon's wives turning away his heart. The standard was fixed before any of it: “Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh” (Gen 2:24).

The larger corruption is the claim that marriage is a social construction which each age may redefine. The Lord Jesus settled the question by going back past Moses to the beginning: “Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female, And said, For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh?” (Mat 19:4-5). Two sexes, one man, one woman, one flesh, joined by God. Everything else — Lamech's two wives, Esau's Canaanite marriages, and every modern redefinition offered since — is measured against that and found to be departure. Esau's marriages were “a grief of mind unto Isaac and to Rebekah” (Gen 26:35), and Scripture expects the reader to feel the same grief.

“Adah bare Jabal” — culture and violence growing on the same branch.
“Adah the daughter of Elon the Hittite” — a marriage that grieved a covenant household.

pos: n. (father of Balaam the soothsayer; the patronymic by which Scripture consistently identifies the prophet who sold his gift)
etymology: From Hebrew Be'or, connected with ba'ar, to burn or consume. Peter's epistle gives the form Bosor, a variant of the same patronymic in Greek transmission.
biblical_def: Beor is known for one thing: he was the father of Balaam, and Scripture almost never names Balaam without him. “Balak sent messengers therefore unto Balaam the son of Beor to Pethor” (Num 22:5); “Balaam the son of Beor hath said, and the man whose eyes are open hath said” (Num 24:3); “Balaam also the son of Beor they slew with the sword” (Num 31:8); and Peter, warning of false teachers, “following the way of Balaam the son of Bosor, who loved the wages of unrighteousness” (2Pe 2:15). The persistence of the patronymic is worth noticing. It marks Balaam as a known man from a known family, a professional diviner of standing whose reputation was sufficient for a king of Moab to send across the Euphrates for him. That is what makes his case so terrible. He was not a charlatan on the margins; he heard the word of the LORD, spoke four oracles of genuine prophecy that no man has improved on, blessed Israel four times against his own interest — and then, unable to curse them, taught Balak how to seduce them into fornication and idolatry at Peor, and died in the slaughter of the Midianites among the enemies of the people he had blessed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Beor; in sacred history he is the father of Balaam the soothsayer, and gives the name by which Balaam is constantly known.
webster_full: BEOR, n. The father of Balaam, who was called by Balak to curse Israel.
The son is almost always styled Balaam the son of Beor, in the law, the prophets and the New Testament.
Peter writes the name Bosor, in the Greek form.
The family dwelt at Pethor, by the river, in the land of the children of his people.
A king of Edom of the same name is mentioned in the book of Genesis.
scriptures: Num 22:5

He sent messengers therefore unto Balaam the son of Beor to Pethor, which is by the river of the land of the children of his people, to call him, saying, Behold, there is a people come out from Egypt: behold, they cover the face of the earth, and they abide over against me:
Num 24:3
And he took up his parable, and said, Balaam the son of Beor hath said, and the man whose eyes are open hath said:
Num 31:8

And they slew the kings of Midian, beside the rest of them that were slain; namely, Evi, and Rekem, and Zur, and Hur, and Reba, five kings of Midian: Balaam also the son of Beor they slew with the sword.
Which have forsaken the right way, and are gone astray, following the way of Balaam the son of Bosor, who loved the wages of unrighteousness;
corruption_summary: Balaam is rehabilitated as a well-meaning pagan seer, and his splendid oracles are used to prove he was a true prophet — when the New Testament names him three times as the pattern of the mercenary teacher.
corruption_paragraphs: Because Balaam son of Beor spoke true prophecy — and magnificent prophecy, including “God is not a man, that he should lie” (Num 23:19) and the star out of Jacob — readers regularly conclude that he was a servant of God who merely stumbled. The New Testament forecloses the reading with unusual force, naming him in three separate books: the error of Balaam for reward (Jud 1:11), the doctrine of Balaam who taught Balak to cast a stumblingblock before Israel (Rev 2:14), and the way of Balaam who loved the wages of unrighteousness (2Pe 2:15). Numbers itself supplies the verdict he never spoke aloud: it was “through the counsel of Balaam” that Israel fell at Peor (Num 31:16). A man may prophesy truly and perish; gifts are not grace.

The second corruption is subtler, and it is a corruption of pastors more than of scholars: the assumption that a right message licenses a wrong motive. Balaam said the right words the whole way through. He even said the right words about money — “If Balak would give me his house full of silver and gold, I cannot go beyond the word of the LORD my God” (Num 22:18) — while going back to ask God a second time about an offer already refused. The heart was for hire and the mouth was orthodox. That is why Peter uses him against false teachers who make merchandise of the flock, and why Paul insisted on handling the churches' money before many witnesses, “providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men” (2Co 8:21).

“Who loved the wages of unrighteousness” — the apostolic verdict on a true oracle for hire.

pos: n. (son of Esau by Bashemath, and head of four dukes of Edom; the same name is borne by the Midianite priest whom Scripture elsewhere calls Jethro)
etymology: From Hebrew Re'u'el, friend of God, from rea', friend or companion, and 'El, God. Numbers renders the Midianite bearer of the name as Raguel (Num 10:29).
biblical_def: Reuel in the genealogies of Genesis 36 is the son of Esau by his wife Bashemath: “And Adah bare to Esau Eliphaz; and Bashemath bare Reuel” (Gen 36:4). His four sons are named — “Nahath, and Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah” (Gen 36:13) — and each becomes a duke: “these are the dukes that came of Reuel in the land of Edom” (Gen 36:17). So Reuel stands at the head of a quarter of the Edomite nobility, in the chapter Moses devotes to Esau's line before turning for good to Jacob's. The name means friend of God, and it is worth pausing over that in a house where the birthright had been despised: the Edomites kept the name of God in their names long after they had lost any claim on His covenant. A second and unrelated man bears the same name — the priest of Midian who gave Moses his daughter Zipporah, called Reuel in Exodus 2:18 and Raguel in Numbers 10:29, and known throughout the rest of the narrative as Jethro; he has his own entry in this dictionary. The two are distinct men in distinct nations, and the shared name is simply a common one.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Reuel; in sacred history he is a son of Esau by Bashemath, father of four dukes of Edom. The name is also borne by the Midianite priest called Jethro.
webster_full: REUEL, n. The name signifies friend of God.
A son of Esau by Bashemath his wife, named in the generations of Esau in Edom.
His sons were Nahath, Zerah, Shammah and Mizzah, who became dukes in the land of Edom.
The same name belongs to the priest of Midian, the father in law of Moses, elsewhere called Jethro.
In the book of Numbers the Midianite is written Raguel.

And Adah bare to Esau Eliphaz; and Bashemath bare Reuel;
These are the names of Esau's sons; Eliphaz the son of Adah the wife of Esau, Reuel the son of Bashemath the wife of Esau.
And these are the sons of Reuel; Nahath, and Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah: these were the sons of Bashemath Esau's wife.

And these are the sons of Reuel Esau's son; duke Nahath, duke Zerah, duke Shammah, duke Mizzah: these are the dukes that came of Reuel in the land of Edom; these are the sons of Bashemath Esau's wife.
corruption_summary: Shared names and variant forms across the Pentateuch are offered as evidence of stitched-together sources; the plainer explanation is that names were common and that men were known by more than one of them.
corruption_paragraphs: That Moses' father-in-law is called Reuel in one place, Raguel in another and Jethro throughout the rest is a standard exhibit for the documentary theory — different names, therefore different sources spliced by a later editor. The dictionary rejects the theory and offers the ordinary explanation. Men in Scripture regularly carry more than one name: Jacob is Israel, Simon is Peter and Cephas, Saul is Paul, Joseph is Zaphnathpaaneah, Daniel is Belteshazzar. A priest might well have a personal name and a title, and a narrative might use whichever the moment requires. Multiplying hypothetical documents to explain what a single author does routinely in every chapter is not caution; it is a method that has already decided Moses did not write the book.

The second observation is theological, and it belongs to the Edomite Reuel. His name means friend of God, and he was the grandson of Isaac and the son of a man who sold his birthright for a meal. A godly name is not a covenant standing. Edom kept the vocabulary of the faith of Abraham and became the nation that refused Israel passage, rejoiced at Jerusalem's fall, and drew Obadiah's whole prophecy down on itself. The warning is exactly the one John the Baptist gave to men who trusted their descent: “think not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father” (Mat 3:9). Names, pedigree and religious vocabulary save nobody.

pos: n. (son of Amminadab, prince of Judah in the wilderness, brother-in-law of Aaron, and an ancestor of David and of Christ)
etymology: From Hebrew Nachshon, connected with nachash, a serpent, or with a root meaning to divine — a common enough name whose bearer is remembered for order rather than omen. Matthew writes it Naasson.
biblical_def: Nahshon the son of Amminadab is the prince of the tribe of Judah in the wilderness, and everything recorded of him has to do with going first. When the tribes are numbered he heads the list: “Of Judah; Nahshon the son of Amminadab” (Num 1:7). When the camp is ordered around the tabernacle, his standard is set on the east, toward the sunrise, and “Nahshon the son of Amminadab shall be captain of the children of Judah” (Num 2:3). When the princes bring their offerings at the dedication of the altar, “he that offered his offering the first day was Nahshon the son of Amminadab, of the tribe of Judah” (Num 7:12). When the camp moves, “in the first place went the standard of the camp of the children of Judah… and over his host was Nahshon” (Num 10:14). First in the count, first in the camp, first to give, first to march. His sister Elisheba married Aaron (Exo 6:23), so the priestly house and the royal tribe were joined in his generation. And the genealogy of Ruth carries him forward: “Amminadab begat Nahshon, and Nahshon begat Salmon” (Rut 4:20) — Salmon who married Rahab, and so to Boaz, Obed, Jesse and David, and at last to Matthew's “Naasson begat Salmon” in the line of Christ.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Nahshon; in sacred history he is the son of Amminadab, prince of the tribe of Judah in the wilderness, and an ancestor of David.
webster_full: NAHSHON, n. The son of Amminadab, and prince or captain of the tribe of Judah.
He was numbered first among the princes at Sinai, and his standard was pitched on the east of the tabernacle.
He offered his offering the first day at the dedication of the altar.
His sister Elisheba was the wife of Aaron the high priest.
He begat Salmon, and is reckoned in the genealogy of David and of our Lord, where the name is written Naasson.

Num 2:3

And on the east side toward the rising of the sun shall they of the standard of the camp of Judah pitch throughout their armies: and Nahshon the son of Amminadab shall be captain of the children of Judah.
Num 7:12
And he that offered his offering the first day was Nahshon the son of Amminadab, of the tribe of Judah:
Rut 4:20

corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this name. The principle to recover is that God appoints order and precedence in His own house, and that faithfulness in an assigned place is what Scripture records.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Nahshon is a wilderness prince whose whole recorded life is the discharge of an office, and no movement has troubled to distort him. What his record does press against is the modern instinct that order is oppression — that assigned places, fixed precedence and appointed leaders are arrangements of power rather than gifts of God. Numbers is a book of order from beginning to end: every tribe counted, every standard placed, every family assigned its side of the tabernacle and its burden to carry, and the whole camp arranged around the dwelling of God in the middle of it. Nahshon is where that order begins each morning.

The principle to recover is that faithfulness in an appointed station is a real and sufficient calling. Nothing dramatic is told of this man — no battle, no miracle, no recorded speech. He was counted first, camped first, gave first, marched first, and out of his house came David and the Christ. The New Testament keeps the same standard for the church, which is likewise to be ordered rather than improvised: “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40), with elders appointed in every city and each member serving in the place assigned. The reward is not spectacle but the master's word: “Well done, thou good and faithful servant” (Mat 25:21).
